Abu Ubaydah said: "baraqa" with a fatha means "shaqqa" (split). Ibn Ishaq said: it means "khafata" (was dazzled) at death. Mujahid said: this is at death. Al-Hasan said: it is the Day of Resurrection. Abu al-Sammal read "balaqa" with a lam in place of the ra', meaning "infataha" (opened) and "infaraja" (parted). It is said: "balaqa al-bab" and "ablaqtuhu" and "ballaqtuhu," meaning I opened it. This is the view of the lexicographers, except al-Farra', who says "balaqahu" and "ablaqahu" mean he closed it. Tha'lab said: al-Farra' erred in this; it is only "balaqa al-bab" and "ablaqahu" when he opened it. End of quote. It is possible that the lam is a substitute for the ra', as they interchange in some speech, as in their saying "nathara" and "nathala," and "wajara" and "wajila."

﴿Wa-khasafa al-qamar﴾: the majority read it in the active voice. Abu Haywah, Ibn Abi Ablah, Yazid ibn Qutayb and Zayd ibn Ali read it in the passive voice. It is said: "khasafa al-qamar" and "khasafahu Allah," and likewise for the sun. Abu Ubaydah and a group of lexicographers said: "khusuf" and "kusuf" have the same meaning. Ibn Abi Uways said: "kusuf" is the going of part of the light, and "khusuf" is all of it.

﴿Wa-jumi'a al-shamsu wal-qamar﴾: the feminine marker was not attached, because the feminine of the sun is metaphorical, or because of giving precedence to the masculine over the feminine. Al-Kisa'i said: it was construed according to meaning, the estimate being: the two lights or the two radiances were gathered. As for the meaning of their being gathered together, Ata' ibn Yasar said: they will be gathered and cast into the Fire. And on his authority: they will be gathered on the Day of Resurrection and then thrown into the sea, and they will become the great Fire of God. It was said: they will be gathered together in rising from the west, rising black and folded up. Ali and Ibn Abbas said: they will be placed in the light of the veils. It was said: they will come together and not separate, and they will draw near to people so that sweat will overtake them because of the intensity of the heat; the meaning is that their heat is gathered. It was also said: they will be gathered together in the loss of light, so there will be no alternation of night and day.

The majority read "al-mafarr" with a fatha on the mim and the fa': where is the escape? Al-Hasan ibn Ali ibn Abi Talib, al-Hasan ibn Zayd, Ibn Abbas, al-Hasan, Ikrimah, Ayyub al-Sakhtiyani, Kulthum ibn Iyad, Mujahid, Ibn Ya'mur, Hammad ibn Salamah, Abu Raja', Isa, Ibn Abi Ishaq, Abu Haywah, Ibn Abi Ablah and al-Zuhri read it with a kasra on the fa', which denotes the place of escape. Al-Hasan read it with a kasra on the mim and a fatha on the fa'; Ibn Atiyah attributed this to al-Zuhri, meaning one who escapes well. This pattern is most often used for instruments and for descriptions of horses, as in the saying of the poet:

"Charging, fleeing, advancing, retreating, all together."

The apparent reading is that His saying "Kalla la wazar" (Nay! There is no refuge) and "Ila rabbika yawma'idhin al-mustaqarr" (To your Lord on that Day is the place of rest) are part of the speech of man. It was also said that they are part of the speech of God, not reported from man. "Kalla" is a rebuke against seeking escape. "La wazar" means: no refuge. The exegetes explained it as a mountain. Mutarrif ibn al-Shikhkhir said: it was the refuge of the Arabs' flight in their lands, which is why it was used. The reality is that it is a refuge, whether a mountain, a fortress, a weapon, a man, or other than these. ("Ila rabbika yawma'idhin") means: to His judgment on that Day; you say, where is the escape? "Al-mustaqarr" means the state of settling, or the place of settling, of a garden or a fire, by His will, Exalted is He: He admits whom He wills to the Garden and admits whom He wills to the Fire.

﴿Bima qaddama wa-akhkhara﴾: Abdullah and Ibn Abbas said: by what he sent forward in his life and what he left behind of a sunnah that is practised after him. Ibn Abbas also said: by what he sent forward of sins and left behind of acts of obedience. Zayd ibn Aslam said: by what he sent forward of his wealth for himself, and what he left of it for the heir. Al-Nakha'i and Mujahid said: by the first of his deeds and the last of them. Al-Dahhak said: by what he sent forward of an obligation and left behind of an obligation. The apparent reading is to take it in its generality: He informs him of everything he sent forward and everything he left behind, both what the exegetes have mentioned and what they have not mentioned.

"Basirah": a predicate about man, meaning a witness. Qatadah said this, and the ha' is for emphasis. Al-Akhfash said: it is like your saying "fulan 'ibrah" and "hujjah" (so-and-so is a lesson and a proof). It was also said: it is feminine because he meant his limbs, meaning his limbs are a witness against himself. It was also said: "basirah" is a subject with an omitted noun, meaning "'ayn basirah" (a seeing eye), and "'ala nafsihi" is the predicate. The clause is in the place of the predicate about man, and the estimate is: a seeing eye. This is the view of al-Farra', who recited:

"As if upon the man of intellect there is a seeing eye, regarding his place, or a sight he is looking at."

"He is wary until he thinks all people, from fear, do not hide his secrets from them."

On this we prefer that "basirah" be the subject of the prepositional phrase, which is the predicate about man. Do you not see that it has been made the predicate about man by its position? On this view the ta' is the feminine marker. Ibn Abbas interpreted "al-basirah" as the limbs, or the guardian angels. The "ma'adhir" according to the majority means excuses, so the meaning is: even if he brings every excuse with which he defends himself, he is himself the witness against them and the clear proof against them. It was said that "ma'adhir" is the plural of "ma'dhirah." Al-Zamakhshari said: the analogical plural of "ma'dhirah" is "ma'adhir," so "ma'adhir" is not the plural of "ma'dhirah" but a collective noun for it, like "manakir" for "munkar." End of quote. This pattern is not among the patterns of collective nouns; it is among the patterns of broken plurals, like "madhakir" and "malamih," whose singulars are "lamhah" and "dhikr." No one has held that these two are collective nouns; rather it was said they are plurals of "lamhah" and "dhikr" by irregular formation, or they are plurals of a singular that was not spoken, namely "midhkar" and "malmahah." Al-Suddi and al-Dahhak said: "al-ma'adhir" means curtains, in the dialect of Yemen; its singular is "mi'dhar," which prevents seeing the one who is veiled, just as an excuse prevents the punishment for a sin. Al-Zajjaj also said this, meaning: even if he throws down veils intending to conceal his deed, his own self is a witness against him. They cited as evidence that "ma'adhir" means curtains the verse of the poet:

"But she grudged us a single hour at the abode, and she was hung above it with curtains."

It was said: "al-basirah" is the recording angels who write down whatever good or evil occurs, meaning: even if he conceals himself with coverings. If "ma'adhir" is taken from excuse, then the meaning of "wa-law alqa" is: he spoke his excuses and uttered them. It was said: even if he put forward his excuses and submitted. Al-Suddi said: even if he advanced a proof and an excuse. It was said: even if he shifted blame onto one another, as in His exalted saying: "Had you not been, we would have been believers" (Saba 31). "Al-'udhrah" and "al-'udhra" mean "al-ma'dhirah" (excuse). The poet said:

"Indeed, that is an excuse which, if it did not benefit..."

And he said concerning it: there is no excuse for one who denies.

Surah al-Qiyamah is Meccan and has forty verses.

In the name of Allah, the Most Gracious, the Most Merciful.

﴿I swear by the Day of Resurrection,﴾ ﴿and I swear by the self-reproaching soul.﴾ ﴿Does man think that We will not assemble his bones?﴾ ﴿Yes, We are able to put together even his fingertips.﴾ ﴿But man wants to continue in sin before him.﴾ ﴿He asks, "When is the Day of Resurrection?"﴾ ﴿So when the sight is dazzled,﴾ ﴿and the moon is eclipsed,﴾ ﴿and the sun and moon are joined together,﴾ ﴿on that day man will say, "Where is the escape?"﴾ ﴿No! There is no refuge.﴾ ﴿To your Lord, on that day, is the place of rest.﴾ ﴿On that day man will be informed of what he sent forward and what he left behind.﴾ ﴿Rather, man is a witness against himself,﴾ ﴿even if he presents his excuses.﴾ ﴿Do not move your tongue with it [the Qur'an] to hasten it.﴾ [al-Qiyamah: 16] ﴿Indeed, upon Us is its collection and its recitation.﴾ [al-Qiyamah: 17] ﴿So when We have recited it, follow its recitation.﴾ [al-Qiyamah: 18] ﴿Then upon Us is its explanation.﴾ [al-Qiyamah: 19] ﴿No! Rather, you love the hasty life [of this world].﴾ [al-Qiyamah: 20] ﴿And you neglect the Hereafter.﴾ [al-Qiyamah: 21] ﴿Faces on that day will be radiant,﴾ [al-Qiyamah: 22] ﴿looking toward their Lord.﴾ [al-Qiyamah: 23] ﴿And faces on that day will be frowning,﴾ [al-Qiyamah: 24] ﴿thinking that a calamity of the backbone is about to be inflicted upon them.﴾ [al-Qiyamah: 25] ﴿No! When [the soul] reaches the collarbones,﴾ [al-Qiyamah: 26] ﴿and it is said, "Who can cure him?"﴾ [al-Qiyamah: 27] ﴿and he thinks that it is the parting,﴾ [al-Qiyamah: 28] ﴿and the leg is entwined with the leg,﴾ [al-Qiyamah: 29] ﴿to your Lord on that day is the driving.﴾ [al-Qiyamah: 30] ﴿So he neither believed nor prayed,﴾ [al-Qiyamah: 31] ﴿but he denied and turned away.﴾ [al-Qiyamah: 32] ﴿Then he went to his family, swaggering.﴾ [al-Qiyamah: 33] ﴿Woe to you, and woe!﴾ [al-Qiyamah: 34] ﴿Again, woe to you, and woe!﴾ [al-Qiyamah: 35] ﴿Does man think that he will be left neglected?﴾ [al-Qiyamah: 36] ﴿Was he not a drop of semen emitted?﴾ [al-Qiyamah: 37] ﴿Then he became a clinging clot, and He created and proportioned [him],﴾ [al-Qiyamah: 38] ﴿and made of him two sexes, the male and the female.﴾ [al-Qiyamah: 39] ﴿Is not He able to give life to the dead?﴾ [al-Qiyamah: 40].

(Commentary) Bariqa, with a kasra on the ra', means he was frightened and bewildered. Its origin is from "bariqa al-rajul," when a man looked at lightning and his sight was dazzled. From this is the verse of Dhu al-Rummah:

"Even if Luqman the Wise were confronted, with Mayy unveiled before his eyes, he would nearly be dazzled."

Al-A'sha said:

"I used to see in the face of Mayya a glimpse, so I would be dazzled, fainting in my place."

Baraqa, with a fatha on the ra', means his sight was split; it comes from al-bariq (glitter), meaning his sight gleamed from the intensity of its staring. Al-wizr is what one takes refuge in, such as a fortress, a mountain, or other things. The poet said:

"By your life, there is no refuge for the youth from death, which overtakes him, and from old age."

Al-nadrah is blessing and the beauty and freshness of the complexion. The poet said:

"A grave that is never absent from my sight has come to me, and a blow of an axe over my head, a crushing one [fāqirah]."

That is: an effective one. Al-taraqi is the plural of taraqwah, which are the bones of the chest; each person has two taraqwahs, and it is the place of the death rattle. Duraid ibn al-Simmah said:

"How many a great matter have I defended on their behalf, when their souls had reached the collarbones."

Raqa yarqi, from al-ruqyah, is what is used to seek healing for the sick through words prepared for that purpose. Tamatta means he swaggered in his walk; its origin is from al-mata, which is the back, meaning he twisted his back in swaggering. It was also said: its origin is tamaṭṭaṭa, meaning he stretched in his walk and extended his shoulders; the ṭā' in it was changed to a weak letter (ḥarf ʿillah) out of dislike for the juxtaposition of similar letters, as they say tazannā from al-ẓann, whose origin is tazannana. Al-maṭīṭā is swaggering and the stretching of the hands while walking; al-maṭīṭ is the stagnant water at the bottom of a pool, because it stretches (yatamaṭṭaṭu) in it, meaning it extends. On this derivation, its origin is not from al-maṭṭ, because the two roots differ: the root of al-mata is (m-ṭ-w) and the root of tamaṭṭaṭa is (m-ṭ-ṭ). Sudan means neglected; it is said "ibil sudan," meaning camels left neglected, grazing wherever they wish without a herder. "Asdaytu al-shay'" means I neglected it, and "asdaytu hajati" means I wasted my need. The poet said:

"I swear by God with the utmost oath, that God has not created anything in vain [sudan]."

Abu Bakr ibn Duraid said in al-Maqsurah:

"I have not seen like the clouds, flocks of camels without markings, which you think are pastured while they are sudan (neglected)."

﴿I swear by the Day of Resurrection,﴾ ﴿and I swear by the self-reproaching soul.﴾ ﴿Does man think that We will not assemble his bones?﴾ ﴿Yes, We are able to put together even his fingertips.﴾ ﴿But man wants to continue in sin before him.﴾ ﴿He asks, "When is the Day of Resurrection?"﴾ ﴿So when the sight is dazzled,﴾ ﴿and the moon is eclipsed,﴾ ﴿and the sun and moon are joined together,﴾ ﴿on that day man will say, "Where is the escape?"﴾ ﴿No! There is no refuge.﴾ ﴿To your Lord, on that day, is the place of rest.﴾ ﴿On that day man will be informed of what he sent forward and what he left behind.﴾ ﴿Rather, man is a witness against himself,﴾ ﴿even if he presents his excuses.﴾ ﴿Do not move your tongue with it [the Qur'an] to hasten it.﴾ [al-Qiyamah: 16] ﴿Indeed, upon Us is its collection and its recitation.﴾ [al-Qiyamah: 17] ﴿So when We have recited it, follow its recitation.﴾ [al-Qiyamah: 18] ﴿Then upon Us is its explanation.﴾ [al-Qiyamah: 19] ﴿No! Rather, you love the hasty life [of this world].﴾ [al-Qiyamah: 20] ﴿And you neglect the Hereafter.﴾ [al-Qiyamah: 21] ﴿Faces on that day will be radiant,﴾ [al-Qiyamah: 22] ﴿looking toward their Lord.﴾ [al-Qiyamah: 23] ﴿And faces on that day will be frowning,﴾ [al-Qiyamah: 24] ﴿thinking that a calamity of the backbone is about to be inflicted upon them.﴾ [al-Qiyamah: 25] ﴿No! When [the soul] reaches the collarbones,﴾ [al-Qiyamah: 26] ﴿and it is said, "Who can cure him?"﴾ [al-Qiyamah: 27] ﴿and he thinks that it is the parting,﴾ [al-Qiyamah: 28] ﴿and the leg is entwined with the leg,﴾ [al-Qiyamah: 29] ﴿to your Lord on that day is the driving.﴾ [al-Qiyamah: 30] ﴿So he neither believed nor prayed,﴾ [al-Qiyamah: 31] ﴿but he denied and turned away.﴾ [al-Qiyamah: 32] ﴿Then he went to his family, swaggering.﴾ [al-Qiyamah: 33] ﴿Woe to you, and woe!﴾ [al-Qiyamah: 34] ﴿Again, woe to you, and woe!﴾ [al-Qiyamah: 35] ﴿Does man think that he will be left neglected?﴾ [al-Qiyamah: 36] ﴿Was he not a drop of semen emitted?﴾ [al-Qiyamah: 37] ﴿Then he became a clinging clot, and He created and proportioned [him],﴾ [al-Qiyamah: 38] ﴿and made of him two sexes, the male and the female.﴾ [al-Qiyamah: 39] ﴿Is not He able to give life to the dead?﴾ [al-Qiyamah: 40].

This surah is Meccan, and its connection to what precedes it is that at the end of the previous surah He says: ﴿No! Rather, they do not fear the Hereafter.﴾ [al-Muddaththir: 53] ﴿No! Indeed, it is a reminder.﴾ [al-Muddaththir: 54] It contains much about the conditions of the Resurrection, so here He mentions the Day of Resurrection and some of its conditions. The discussion of ﴿I do not swear﴾ has already been covered, as well as the disagreement over "lā" and the disagreement over its readings at the end of al-Waqi'ah. God swore by the Day of Resurrection because of its greatness and terror. As for ﴿lā uqsimu﴾, it has been said that "lā" is negative: He denies that He swears by the self-reproaching soul, and swears by the Day of Resurrection; al-Hasan stated this. The majority hold that God swore by both things.

As for al-lawwāmah, al-Hasan said it is the one that blames its owner for abandoning obedience and similar matters; in this sense it is praiseworthy, and that is why God swore by it. Something similar is reported from Ibn 'Abbas and Mujahid: it blames for what has passed and regrets evil, asking why it did it, and regrets good, asking why it did not increase it. It was also said that it is the God-fearing soul that blames souls on the Day of Resurrection for their shortcomings in piety. Ibn 'Abbas and Qatadah said it is the wicked, disquieted soul that blames its owner for what he missed of the worldly striving and its goods; in this sense it is blameworthy, and it is fitting that the oath by it be negated. Al-nafs al-lawwamah is a generic noun with this attribute. It was also said that it is a specific soul, namely the soul of Adam, peace be upon him, which never ceased to blame him for his action that caused his expulsion from the Garden. Ibn 'Atiyyah said: every soul that is intermediate, neither at peace nor commanding evil, is lawwamah in both directions: at times it blames for abandoning obedience, and at times it blames for missing what it desires. When it becomes at peace, it becomes pure and clear. End of quote.

The connection between the two oaths lies in the states of the soul, its happiness and its wretchedness, and the manifestation of that on the Day of Resurrection. The answer to the oath is omitted, and what indicates it is the Day of Resurrection, which is sworn by, and what follows it in His words: ﴿Does man think﴾, and its estimated meaning is: "You will surely be resurrected."

Al-Zamakhshari said: If you say, God's words ﴿But no, by your Lord, they do not believe﴾ [al-Nisa': 65], and the verses you recited, the sworn matter in them is negated, and he had recited the words of Imru' al-Qays:

"No, by your father, daughter of al-'Amiri, the people do not claim that I flee."

And the words of Ghuwayyah ibn Sulma:

"Umamah called out, to burden me, so let me not care."

He said: Why did you not claim that the "lā" used for the oath was added as a preface to negation after it and as its emphasis, and estimate the omitted sworn matter here as negative, like your saying: ﴿I do not swear by the Day of Resurrection﴾, you will not be left neglected? I said: If they had restricted the matter to negation without affirmation, this statement would have had some basis, but He did not swear. Do you not see how He linked ﴿I do not swear by this city﴾ [al-Balad: 1] with His words ﴿Certainly We created man in hardship﴾ [al-Balad: 4]? And similarly ﴿So I do not swear by the positions of the stars﴾ [al-Waqi'ah: 75] ﴿Indeed, it is a noble Qur'an﴾ [al-Waqi'ah: 77]? Then al-Zamakhshari said: The answer to the oath is what His words ﴿Does man think that We will not assemble his bones﴾ indicate, and it is: "you will surely be resurrected." End of quote. This is also the estimate of al-Nahhas. The view of one who said the answer to the oath is ﴿Does man think﴾, and what is reported from al-Hasan that the answer is ﴿Yes, We are able﴾, and what was said that "lā" in both oaths is for negating them, meaning "I do not swear about anything," and that the estimate is "I ask you: does man think?", are sayings not fit to be adopted; rather they are discarded and paper should not be blackened with them. Had they not been recorded in books, I would not have pointed them out.

Al-insan here means the disbelieving denier of the Resurrection. It is reported that 'Adi ibn Rabi'ah said to the Messenger of God ﷺ: "O Muhammad, tell me about the Day of Resurrection: when will its matter be?" The Messenger of God ﷺ informed him, and he said: "Had I witnessed that day, I would not (p-385) have believed you or believed in it, or [do you claim] that God will gather these bones after their decay?" Then it was revealed. It was also said that it was revealed concerning Abu Jahl, who used to say: "Does Muhammad claim that God will gather these bones after their decay and dispersal, and restore them as a new creation?"

The majority read ﴿najma'a﴾ with "n" and ﴿'izāmahu﴾ in the accusative. Qatadah read it with "t", in the passive voice, and ﴿'izāmuhu﴾ in the nominative; the meaning is: after their dispersal, their mixing with the dust, and the winds scattering them to the far ends of the earth.

His words ﴿Does man think﴾ are an interrogative of affirmation and reproach, in which he denies God's power to restore what is non-existent. ﴿Balā﴾ is the answer to the interrogative that extends to the negation, meaning: "Yes, We will gather them." He mentioned the bones, although the meaning is the restoration of the person and the gathering of his scattered parts, because the bones are the mold of creation.

The majority read ﴿qādirīn﴾ with the accusative as a state (ḥāl) of the pronoun in the implied verb, which is "yajma'uhā" (He gathers them). Ibn Abi 'Abla and Ibn al-Sumayqa read ﴿qādirūn﴾, meaning "We are able."

﴿To put together his fingertips﴾: these are the fingers, the bones most scattered and most finely divided, the bones in the fingertips and their joints; this is at the resurrection. Ibn 'Abbas and the majority said the meaning is: We will make them in his present life a single piece, or a single bone like a camel's sole, with no separations in it, meaning in this world, so that his benefit from them becomes small. This view contains a threat. The first meaning is the apparent one and the intended purpose of the arrangement of the speech. Al-Zamakhshari mentioned these two views with polished wording, in keeping with his habit of relating the views of earlier scholars. It was also said: ﴿qādirīn﴾ is accusative as the predicate of "kāna," meaning: "Yes, we were able at the beginning."

Nay, but man desires to continue in sin (lit. "Nay, but man wishes"): "Bal" (nay, but) is a particle of disengagement (idrab), which is a transition from one statement to another without negating the first. The apparent sense is that "yurid" (desires) is a report about what man desires. Al-Zamakhshari said: "Bal yurid" is coordinated with "ayahsabu" (does man think...), so it may be preceded by an interrogative and may be affirmative, turning away from one questioned matter to another, or turning away from a questioned matter to an affirmative one. End of quote. These three estimations do not appear clearly; they are forced. Rather, the meaning is a report about man without negating the content of the preceding sentence, which is "We are able to gather his bones" (cf. verse 4), in order to show what man is like: his lack of thought about the Hereafter and that he is preoccupied with his desires. The object of "yurid" is omitted, indicated by the causal clause in "liyafjura" (so that he may commit wickedness). Mujahid, al-Hasan, Ikrimah, Ibn Jubayr, al-Dahhak and al-Suddi said: the meaning of the verse is that man only desires his lusts and his sins, so that he may continue in them forever, heedlessly driving forward, obeying his hopes and postponing repentance. Al-Suddi also said: so that he may do wrong to the extent of his capacity. On this view the pronoun in "amamahu" (before him) refers to man, which is the apparent reading. Ibn Abbas said something implying that the pronoun refers to the Day of Resurrection: that man, during his lifetime, is "amam" (in front of) the Day of Resurrection, and "bayna yadayhi" (before him) is the Day of Resurrection, behind him. So he desires his lusts, so that he may commit wickedness by denying the resurrection and other matters before the Day of Resurrection, and he does not know the state he is in. "Al-amam" (in front) is a noun of place, here used metaphorically for time, meaning: so that he may commit wickedness in what lies before him and awaits him of the time of his life.

﴿Yas'alu ayyana yawmu al-qiyamah﴾ means: when is the Day of Resurrection? It is a question of mockery, denial and obstinacy. The majority read "baraqa" with a kasra on the ra'. Zayd ibn Thabit, Nasr ibn Asim, Abdullah ibn Abi Ishaq, Abu Haywah, Ibn Abi Ablah, al-Za'farani, Ibn Miqsam, Nafi', Zayd ibn Ali, Aban on the authority of Asim, Harun and Mahbub (both on the authority of Abu Amr), al-Hasan and al-Jahdari read it with a fatha, in differing reports from them. Abu Ubaydah said: "baraqa" with a fatha means "shaqqa" (split). Ibn Ishaq said: it means "khafata" (was dazzled) at death. Mujahid said: this is at death. Al-Hasan said: it is the Day of Resurrection. Abu al-Sammal read "balaqa" with a lam in place of the ra', meaning "infataha" (opened) and "infaraja" (parted). It is said: "balaqa al-bab" and "ablaqtuhu" and "ballaqtuhu," meaning I opened it. This is the view of the lexicographers, except al-Farra', who says "balaqahu" and "ablaqahu" mean he closed it. Tha'lab said: al-Farra' erred in this; it is only "balaqa al-bab" and "ablaqahu" when he opened it. End of quote. It is possible that the lam is a substitute for the ra', as they interchange in some speech, as in their saying "nathara" and "nathala," and "wajara" and "wajila."

﴿Wa-khasafa al-qamar﴾: the majority read it in the active voice. Abu Haywah, Ibn Abi Ablah, Yazid ibn Qutayb and Zayd ibn Ali read it in the passive voice. It is said: "khasafa al-qamar" and "khasafahu Allah," and likewise for the sun. Abu Ubaydah and a group of lexicographers said: "khusuf" and "kusuf" have the same meaning. Ibn Abi Uways said: "kusuf" is the going of part of the light, and "khusuf" is all of it.

﴿Wa-jumi'a al-shamsu wal-qamar﴾: the feminine marker was not attached, because the feminine of the sun is metaphorical, or because of giving precedence to the masculine over the feminine. Al-Kisa'i said: it was construed according to meaning, the estimate being: the two lights or the two radiances were gathered. As for the meaning of their being gathered together, Ata' ibn Yasar said: they will be gathered and cast into the Fire. And on his authority: they will be gathered on the Day of Resurrection and then thrown into the sea, and they will become the great Fire of God. It was said: they will be gathered together in rising from the west, rising black and folded up. Ali and Ibn Abbas said: they will be placed in the light of the veils. It was said: they will come together and not separate, and they will draw near to people so that sweat will overtake them because of the intensity of the heat; the meaning is that their heat is gathered. It was also said: they will be gathered together in the loss of light, so there will be no alternation of night and day.

The majority read "al-mafarr" with a fatha on the mim and the fa': where is the escape? Al-Hasan ibn Ali ibn Abi Talib, al-Hasan ibn Zayd, Ibn Abbas, al-Hasan, Ikrimah, Ayyub al-Sakhtiyani, Kulthum ibn Iyad, Mujahid, Ibn Ya'mur, Hammad ibn Salamah, Abu Raja', Isa, Ibn Abi Ishaq, Abu Haywah, Ibn Abi Ablah and al-Zuhri read it with a kasra on the fa', which denotes the place of escape. Al-Hasan read it with a kasra on the mim and a fatha on the fa'; Ibn Atiyah attributed this to al-Zuhri, meaning one who escapes well. This pattern is most often used for instruments and for descriptions of horses, as in the saying of the poet:

"Charging, fleeing, advancing, retreating, all together."

The apparent reading is that His saying "Kalla la wazar" (Nay! There is no refuge) and "Ila rabbika yawma'idhin al-mustaqarr" (To your Lord on that Day is the place of rest) are part of the speech of man. It was also said that they are part of the speech of God, not reported from man. "Kalla" is a rebuke against seeking escape. "La wazar" means: no refuge. The exegetes explained it as a mountain. Mutarrif ibn al-Shikhkhir said: it was the refuge of the Arabs' flight in their lands, which is why it was used. The reality is that it is a refuge, whether a mountain, a fortress, a weapon, a man, or other than these. ("Ila rabbika yawma'idhin") means: to His judgment on that Day; you say, where is the escape? "Al-mustaqarr" means the state of settling, or the place of settling, of a garden or a fire, by His will, Exalted is He: He admits whom He wills to the Garden and admits whom He wills to the Fire.

﴿Bima qaddama wa-akhkhara﴾: Abdullah and Ibn Abbas said: by what he sent forward in his life and what he left behind of a sunnah that is practised after him. Ibn Abbas also said: by what he sent forward of sins and left behind of acts of obedience. Zayd ibn Aslam said: by what he sent forward of his wealth for himself, and what he left of it for the heir. Al-Nakha'i and Mujahid said: by the first of his deeds and the last of them. Al-Dahhak said: by what he sent forward of an obligation and left behind of an obligation. The apparent reading is to take it in its generality: He informs him of everything he sent forward and everything he left behind, both what the exegetes have mentioned and what they have not mentioned.

"Basirah": a predicate about man, meaning a witness. Qatadah said this, and the ha' is for emphasis. Al-Akhfash said: it is like your saying "fulan 'ibrah" and "hujjah" (so-and-so is a lesson and a proof). It was also said: it is feminine because he meant his limbs, meaning his limbs are a witness against himself. It was also said: "basirah" is a subject with an omitted noun, meaning "'ayn basirah" (a seeing eye), and "'ala nafsihi" is the predicate. The clause is in the place of the predicate about man, and the estimate is: a seeing eye. This is the view of al-Farra', who recited:

"As if upon the man of intellect there is a seeing eye, regarding his place, or a sight he is looking at."

"He is wary until he thinks all people, from fear, do not hide his secrets from them."

On this we prefer that "basirah" be the subject of the prepositional phrase, which is the predicate about man. Do you not see that it has been made the predicate about man by its position? On this view the ta' is the feminine marker. Ibn Abbas interpreted "al-basirah" as the limbs, or the guardian angels. The "ma'adhir" according to the majority means excuses, so the meaning is: even if he brings every excuse with which he defends himself, he is himself the witness against them and the clear proof against them. It was said that "ma'adhir" is the plural of "ma'dhirah." Al-Zamakhshari said: the analogical plural of "ma'dhirah" is "ma'adhir," so "ma'adhir" is not the plural of "ma'dhirah" but a collective noun for it, like "manakir" for "munkar." End of quote. This pattern is not among the patterns of collective nouns; it is among the patterns of broken plurals, like "madhakir" and "malamih," whose singulars are "lamhah" and "dhikr." No one has held that these two are collective nouns; rather it was said they are plurals of "lamhah" and "dhikr" by irregular formation, or they are plurals of a singular that was not spoken, namely "midhkar" and "malmahah." Al-Suddi and al-Dahhak said: "al-ma'adhir" means curtains, in the dialect of Yemen; its singular is "mi'dhar," which prevents seeing the one who is veiled, just as an excuse prevents the punishment for a sin. Al-Zajjaj also said this, meaning: even if he throws down veils intending to conceal his deed, his own self is a witness against him. They cited as evidence that "ma'adhir" means curtains the verse of the poet:

"But she grudged us a single hour at the abode, and she was hung above it with curtains."

It was said: "al-basirah" is the recording angels who write down whatever good or evil occurs, meaning: even if he conceals himself with coverings. If "ma'adhir" is taken from excuse, then the meaning of "wa-law alqa" is: he spoke his excuses and uttered them. It was said: even if he put forward his excuses and submitted. Al-Suddi said: even if he advanced a proof and an excuse. It was said: even if he shifted blame onto one another, as in His exalted saying: "Had you not been, we would have been believers" (Saba 31). "Al-'udhrah" and "al-'udhra" mean "al-ma'dhirah" (excuse). The poet said:

"Indeed, that is an excuse which, if it did not benefit..."

And he said concerning it: there is no excuse for one who denies.

Surah al-Qiyamah is Meccan and has forty verses.

In the name of Allah, the Most Gracious, the Most Merciful.

﴿I swear by the Day of Resurrection,﴾ ﴿and I swear by the self-reproaching soul.﴾ ﴿Does man think that We will not assemble his bones?﴾ ﴿Yes, We are able to put together even his fingertips.﴾ ﴿But man wants to continue in sin before him.﴾ ﴿He asks, "When is the Day of Resurrection?"﴾ ﴿So when the sight is dazzled,﴾ ﴿and the moon is eclipsed,﴾ ﴿and the sun and moon are joined together,﴾ ﴿on that day man will say, "Where is the escape?"﴾ ﴿No! There is no refuge.﴾ ﴿To your Lord, on that day, is the place of rest.﴾ ﴿On that day man will be informed of what he sent forward and what he left behind.﴾ ﴿Rather, man is a witness against himself,﴾ ﴿even if he presents his excuses.﴾ ﴿Do not move your tongue with it [the Qur'an] to hasten it.﴾ [al-Qiyamah: 16] ﴿Indeed, upon Us is its collection and its recitation.﴾ [al-Qiyamah: 17] ﴿So when We have recited it, follow its recitation.﴾ [al-Qiyamah: 18] ﴿Then upon Us is its explanation.﴾ [al-Qiyamah: 19] ﴿No! Rather, you love the hasty life [of this world].﴾ [al-Qiyamah: 20] ﴿And you neglect the Hereafter.﴾ [al-Qiyamah: 21] ﴿Faces on that day will be radiant,﴾ [al-Qiyamah: 22] ﴿looking toward their Lord.﴾ [al-Qiyamah: 23] ﴿And faces on that day will be frowning,﴾ [al-Qiyamah: 24] ﴿thinking that a calamity of the backbone is about to be inflicted upon them.﴾ [al-Qiyamah: 25] ﴿No! When [the soul] reaches the collarbones,﴾ [al-Qiyamah: 26] ﴿and it is said, "Who can cure him?"﴾ [al-Qiyamah: 27] ﴿and he thinks that it is the parting,﴾ [al-Qiyamah: 28] ﴿and the leg is entwined with the leg,﴾ [al-Qiyamah: 29] ﴿to your Lord on that day is the driving.﴾ [al-Qiyamah: 30] ﴿So he neither believed nor prayed,﴾ [al-Qiyamah: 31] ﴿but he denied and turned away.﴾ [al-Qiyamah: 32] ﴿Then he went to his family, swaggering.﴾ [al-Qiyamah: 33] ﴿Woe to you, and woe!﴾ [al-Qiyamah: 34] ﴿Again, woe to you, and woe!﴾ [al-Qiyamah: 35] ﴿Does man think that he will be left neglected?﴾ [al-Qiyamah: 36] ﴿Was he not a drop of semen emitted?﴾ [al-Qiyamah: 37] ﴿Then he became a clinging clot, and He created and proportioned [him],﴾ [al-Qiyamah: 38] ﴿and made of him two sexes, the male and the female.﴾ [al-Qiyamah: 39] ﴿Is not He able to give life to the dead?﴾ [al-Qiyamah: 40].

(Commentary) Bariqa, with a kasra on the ra', means he was frightened and bewildered. Its origin is from "bariqa al-rajul," when a man looked at lightning and his sight was dazzled. From this is the verse of Dhu al-Rummah:

"Even if Luqman the Wise were confronted, with Mayy unveiled before his eyes, he would nearly be dazzled."

Al-A'sha said:

"I used to see in the face of Mayya a glimpse, so I would be dazzled, fainting in my place."

Baraqa, with a fatha on the ra', means his sight was split; it comes from al-bariq (glitter), meaning his sight gleamed from the intensity of its staring. Al-wizr is what one takes refuge in, such as a fortress, a mountain, or other things. The poet said:

"By your life, there is no refuge for the youth from death, which overtakes him, and from old age."

Al-nadrah is blessing and the beauty and freshness of the complexion. The poet said:

"A grave that is never absent from my sight has come to me, and a blow of an axe over my head, a crushing one [fāqirah]."

That is: an effective one. Al-taraqi is the plural of taraqwah, which are the bones of the chest; each person has two taraqwahs, and it is the place of the death rattle. Duraid ibn al-Simmah said:

"How many a great matter have I defended on their behalf, when their souls had reached the collarbones."

Raqa yarqi, from al-ruqyah, is what is used to seek healing for the sick through words prepared for that purpose. Tamatta means he swaggered in his walk; its origin is from al-mata, which is the back, meaning he twisted his back in swaggering. It was also said: its origin is tamaṭṭaṭa, meaning he stretched in his walk and extended his shoulders; the ṭā' in it was changed to a weak letter (ḥarf ʿillah) out of dislike for the juxtaposition of similar letters, as they say tazannā from al-ẓann, whose origin is tazannana. Al-maṭīṭā is swaggering and the stretching of the hands while walking; al-maṭīṭ is the stagnant water at the bottom of a pool, because it stretches (yatamaṭṭaṭu) in it, meaning it extends. On this derivation, its origin is not from al-maṭṭ, because the two roots differ: the root of al-mata is (m-ṭ-w) and the root of tamaṭṭaṭa is (m-ṭ-ṭ). Sudan means neglected; it is said "ibil sudan," meaning camels left neglected, grazing wherever they wish without a herder. "Asdaytu al-shay'" means I neglected it, and "asdaytu hajati" means I wasted my need. The poet said:

"I swear by God with the utmost oath, that God has not created anything in vain [sudan]."

Abu Bakr ibn Duraid said in al-Maqsurah:

"I have not seen like the clouds, flocks of camels without markings, which you think are pastured while they are sudan (neglected)."

﴿I swear by the Day of Resurrection,﴾ ﴿and I swear by the self-reproaching soul.﴾ ﴿Does man think that We will not assemble his bones?﴾ ﴿Yes, We are able to put together even his fingertips.﴾ ﴿But man wants to continue in sin before him.﴾ ﴿He asks, "When is the Day of Resurrection?"﴾ ﴿So when the sight is dazzled,﴾ ﴿and the moon is eclipsed,﴾ ﴿and the sun and moon are joined together,﴾ ﴿on that day man will say, "Where is the escape?"﴾ ﴿No! There is no refuge.﴾ ﴿To your Lord, on that day, is the place of rest.﴾ ﴿On that day man will be informed of what he sent forward and what he left behind.﴾ ﴿Rather, man is a witness against himself,﴾ ﴿even if he presents his excuses.﴾ ﴿Do not move your tongue with it [the Qur'an] to hasten it.﴾ [al-Qiyamah: 16] ﴿Indeed, upon Us is its collection and its recitation.﴾ [al-Qiyamah: 17] ﴿So when We have recited it, follow its recitation.﴾ [al-Qiyamah: 18] ﴿Then upon Us is its explanation.﴾ [al-Qiyamah: 19] ﴿No! Rather, you love the hasty life [of this world].﴾ [al-Qiyamah: 20] ﴿And you neglect the Hereafter.﴾ [al-Qiyamah: 21] ﴿Faces on that day will be radiant,﴾ [al-Qiyamah: 22] ﴿looking toward their Lord.﴾ [al-Qiyamah: 23] ﴿And faces on that day will be frowning,﴾ [al-Qiyamah: 24] ﴿thinking that a calamity of the backbone is about to be inflicted upon them.﴾ [al-Qiyamah: 25] ﴿No! When [the soul] reaches the collarbones,﴾ [al-Qiyamah: 26] ﴿and it is said, "Who can cure him?"﴾ [al-Qiyamah: 27] ﴿and he thinks that it is the parting,﴾ [al-Qiyamah: 28] ﴿and the leg is entwined with the leg,﴾ [al-Qiyamah: 29] ﴿to your Lord on that day is the driving.﴾ [al-Qiyamah: 30] ﴿So he neither believed nor prayed,﴾ [al-Qiyamah: 31] ﴿but he denied and turned away.﴾ [al-Qiyamah: 32] ﴿Then he went to his family, swaggering.﴾ [al-Qiyamah: 33] ﴿Woe to you, and woe!﴾ [al-Qiyamah: 34] ﴿Again, woe to you, and woe!﴾ [al-Qiyamah: 35] ﴿Does man think that he will be left neglected?﴾ [al-Qiyamah: 36] ﴿Was he not a drop of semen emitted?﴾ [al-Qiyamah: 37] ﴿Then he became a clinging clot, and He created and proportioned [him],﴾ [al-Qiyamah: 38] ﴿and made of him two sexes, the male and the female.﴾ [al-Qiyamah: 39] ﴿Is not He able to give life to the dead?﴾ [al-Qiyamah: 40].

This surah is Meccan, and its connection to what precedes it is that at the end of the previous surah He says: ﴿No! Rather, they do not fear the Hereafter.﴾ [al-Muddaththir: 53] ﴿No! Indeed, it is a reminder.﴾ [al-Muddaththir: 54] It contains much about the conditions of the Resurrection, so here He mentions the Day of Resurrection and some of its conditions. The discussion of ﴿I do not swear﴾ has already been covered, as well as the disagreement over "lā" and the disagreement over its readings at the end of al-Waqi'ah. God swore by the Day of Resurrection because of its greatness and terror. As for ﴿lā uqsimu﴾, it has been said that "lā" is negative: He denies that He swears by the self-reproaching soul, and swears by the Day of Resurrection; al-Hasan stated this. The majority hold that God swore by both things.

As for al-lawwāmah, al-Hasan said it is the one that blames its owner for abandoning obedience and similar matters; in this sense it is praiseworthy, and that is why God swore by it. Something similar is reported from Ibn 'Abbas and Mujahid: it blames for what has passed and regrets evil, asking why it did it, and regrets good, asking why it did not increase it. It was also said that it is the God-fearing soul that blames souls on the Day of Resurrection for their shortcomings in piety. Ibn 'Abbas and Qatadah said it is the wicked, disquieted soul that blames its owner for what he missed of the worldly striving and its goods; in this sense it is blameworthy, and it is fitting that the oath by it be negated. Al-nafs al-lawwamah is a generic noun with this attribute. It was also said that it is a specific soul, namely the soul of Adam, peace be upon him, which never ceased to blame him for his action that caused his expulsion from the Garden. Ibn 'Atiyyah said: every soul that is intermediate, neither at peace nor commanding evil, is lawwamah in both directions: at times it blames for abandoning obedience, and at times it blames for missing what it desires. When it becomes at peace, it becomes pure and clear. End of quote.

The connection between the two oaths lies in the states of the soul, its happiness and its wretchedness, and the manifestation of that on the Day of Resurrection. The answer to the oath is omitted, and what indicates it is the Day of Resurrection, which is sworn by, and what follows it in His words: ﴿Does man think﴾, and its estimated meaning is: "You will surely be resurrected."

Al-Zamakhshari said: If you say, God's words ﴿But no, by your Lord, they do not believe﴾ [al-Nisa': 65], and the verses you recited, the sworn matter in them is negated, and he had recited the words of Imru' al-Qays:

"No, by your father, daughter of al-'Amiri, the people do not claim that I flee."

And the words of Ghuwayyah ibn Sulma:

"Umamah called out, to burden me, so let me not care."

He said: Why did you not claim that the "lā" used for the oath was added as a preface to negation after it and as its emphasis, and estimate the omitted sworn matter here as negative, like your saying: ﴿I do not swear by the Day of Resurrection﴾, you will not be left neglected? I said: If they had restricted the matter to negation without affirmation, this statement would have had some basis, but He did not swear. Do you not see how He linked ﴿I do not swear by this city﴾ [al-Balad: 1] with His words ﴿Certainly We created man in hardship﴾ [al-Balad: 4]? And similarly ﴿So I do not swear by the positions of the stars﴾ [al-Waqi'ah: 75] ﴿Indeed, it is a noble Qur'an﴾ [al-Waqi'ah: 77]? Then al-Zamakhshari said: The answer to the oath is what His words ﴿Does man think that We will not assemble his bones﴾ indicate, and it is: "you will surely be resurrected." End of quote. This is also the estimate of al-Nahhas. The view of one who said the answer to the oath is ﴿Does man think﴾, and what is reported from al-Hasan that the answer is ﴿Yes, We are able﴾, and what was said that "lā" in both oaths is for negating them, meaning "I do not swear about anything," and that the estimate is "I ask you: does man think?", are sayings not fit to be adopted; rather they are discarded and paper should not be blackened with them. Had they not been recorded in books, I would not have pointed them out.

Al-insan here means the disbelieving denier of the Resurrection. It is reported that 'Adi ibn Rabi'ah said to the Messenger of God ﷺ: "O Muhammad, tell me about the Day of Resurrection: when will its matter be?" The Messenger of God ﷺ informed him, and he said: "Had I witnessed that day, I would not (p-385) have believed you or believed in it, or [do you claim] that God will gather these bones after their decay?" Then it was revealed. It was also said that it was revealed concerning Abu Jahl, who used to say: "Does Muhammad claim that God will gather these bones after their decay and dispersal, and restore them as a new creation?"

The majority read ﴿najma'a﴾ with "n" and ﴿'izāmahu﴾ in the accusative. Qatadah read it with "t", in the passive voice, and ﴿'izāmuhu﴾ in the nominative; the meaning is: after their dispersal, their mixing with the dust, and the winds scattering them to the far ends of the earth.

His words ﴿Does man think﴾ are an interrogative of affirmation and reproach, in which he denies God's power to restore what is non-existent. ﴿Balā﴾ is the answer to the interrogative that extends to the negation, meaning: "Yes, We will gather them." He mentioned the bones, although the meaning is the restoration of the person and the gathering of his scattered parts, because the bones are the mold of creation.

The majority read ﴿qādirīn﴾ with the accusative as a state (ḥāl) of the pronoun in the implied verb, which is "yajma'uhā" (He gathers them). Ibn Abi 'Abla and Ibn al-Sumayqa read ﴿qādirūn﴾, meaning "We are able."

﴿To put together his fingertips﴾: these are the fingers, the bones most scattered and most finely divided, the bones in the fingertips and their joints; this is at the resurrection. Ibn 'Abbas and the majority said the meaning is: We will make them in his present life a single piece, or a single bone like a camel's sole, with no separations in it, meaning in this world, so that his benefit from them becomes small. This view contains a threat. The first meaning is the apparent one and the intended purpose of the arrangement of the speech. Al-Zamakhshari mentioned these two views with polished wording, in keeping with his habit of relating the views of earlier scholars. It was also said: ﴿qādirīn﴾ is accusative as the predicate of "kāna," meaning: "Yes, we were able at the beginning."

Nay, but man desires to continue in sin (lit. "Nay, but man wishes"): "Bal" (nay, but) is a particle of disengagement (idrab), which is a transition from one statement to another without negating the first. The apparent sense is that "yurid" (desires) is a report about what man desires. Al-Zamakhshari said: "Bal yurid" is coordinated with "ayahsabu" (does man think...), so it may be preceded by an interrogative and may be affirmative, turning away from one questioned matter to another, or turning away from a questioned matter to an affirmative one. End of quote. These three estimations do not appear clearly; they are forced. Rather, the meaning is a report about man without negating the content of the preceding sentence, which is "We are able to gather his bones" (cf. verse 4), in order to show what man is like: his lack of thought about the Hereafter and that he is preoccupied with his desires. The object of "yurid" is omitted, indicated by the causal clause in "liyafjura" (so that he may commit wickedness). Mujahid, al-Hasan, Ikrimah, Ibn Jubayr, al-Dahhak and al-Suddi said: the meaning of the verse is that man only desires his lusts and his sins, so that he may continue in them forever, heedlessly driving forward, obeying his hopes and postponing repentance. Al-Suddi also said: so that he may do wrong to the extent of his capacity. On this view the pronoun in "amamahu" (before him) refers to man, which is the apparent reading. Ibn Abbas said something implying that the pronoun refers to the Day of Resurrection: that man, during his lifetime, is "amam" (in front of) the Day of Resurrection, and "bayna yadayhi" (before him) is the Day of Resurrection, behind him. So he desires his lusts, so that he may commit wickedness by denying the resurrection and other matters before the Day of Resurrection, and he does not know the state he is in. "Al-amam" (in front) is a noun of place, here used metaphorically for time, meaning: so that he may commit wickedness in what lies before him and awaits him of the time of his life.

﴿Yas'alu ayyana yawmu al-qiyamah﴾ means: when is the Day of Resurrection? It is a question of mockery, denial and obstinacy. The majority read "baraqa" with a kasra on the ra'. Zayd ibn Thabit, Nasr ibn Asim, Abdullah ibn Abi Ishaq, Abu Haywah, Ibn Abi Ablah, al-Za'farani, Ibn Miqsam, Nafi', Zayd ibn Ali, Aban on the authority of Asim, Harun and Mahbub (both on the authority of Abu Amr), al-Hasan and al-Jahdari read it with a fatha, in differing reports from them. Abu Ubaydah said: "baraqa" with a fatha means "shaqqa" (split). Ibn Ishaq said: it means "khafata" (was dazzled) at death. Mujahid said: this is at death. Al-Hasan said: it is the Day of Resurrection. Abu al-Sammal read "balaqa" with a lam in place of the ra', meaning "infataha" (opened) and "infaraja" (parted). It is said: "balaqa al-bab" and "ablaqtuhu" and "ballaqtuhu," meaning I opened it. This is the view of the lexicographers, except al-Farra', who says "balaqahu" and "ablaqahu" mean he closed it. Tha'lab said: al-Farra' erred in this; it is only "balaqa al-bab" and "ablaqahu" when he opened it. End of quote. It is possible that the lam is a substitute for the ra', as they interchange in some speech, as in their saying "nathara" and "nathala," and "wajara" and "wajila."

﴿Wa-khasafa al-qamar﴾: the majority read it in the active voice. Abu Haywah, Ibn Abi Ablah, Yazid ibn Qutayb and Zayd ibn Ali read it in the passive voice. It is said: "khasafa al-qamar" and "khasafahu Allah," and likewise for the sun. Abu Ubaydah and a group of lexicographers said: "khusuf" and "kusuf" have the same meaning. Ibn Abi Uways said: "kusuf" is the going of part of the light, and "khusuf" is all of it.

﴿Wa-jumi'a al-shamsu wal-qamar﴾: the feminine marker was not attached, because the feminine of the sun is metaphorical, or because of giving precedence to the masculine over the feminine. Al-Kisa'i said: it was construed according to meaning, the estimate being: the two lights or the two radiances were gathered. As for the meaning of their being gathered together, Ata' ibn Yasar said: they will be gathered and cast into the Fire. And on his authority: they will be gathered on the Day of Resurrection and then thrown into the sea, and they will become the great Fire of God. It was said: they will be gathered together in rising from the west, rising black and folded up. Ali and Ibn Abbas said: they will be placed in the light of the veils. It was said: they will come together and not separate, and they will draw near to people so that sweat will overtake them because of the intensity of the heat; the meaning is that their heat is gathered. It was also said: they will be gathered together in the loss of light, so there will be no alternation of night and day.

The majority read "al-mafarr" with a fatha on the mim and the fa': where is the escape? Al-Hasan ibn Ali ibn Abi Talib, al-Hasan ibn Zayd, Ibn Abbas, al-Hasan, Ikrimah, Ayyub al-Sakhtiyani, Kulthum ibn Iyad, Mujahid, Ibn Ya'mur, Hammad ibn Salamah, Abu Raja', Isa, Ibn Abi Ishaq, Abu Haywah, Ibn Abi Ablah and al-Zuhri read it with a kasra on the fa', which denotes the place of escape. Al-Hasan read it with a kasra on the mim and a fatha on the fa'; Ibn Atiyah attributed this to al-Zuhri, meaning one who escapes well. This pattern is most often used for instruments and for descriptions of horses, as in the saying of the poet:

"Charging, fleeing, advancing, retreating, all together."

The apparent reading is that His saying "Kalla la wazar" (Nay! There is no refuge) and "Ila rabbika yawma'idhin al-mustaqarr" (To your Lord on that Day is the place of rest) are part of the speech of man. It was also said that they are part of the speech of God, not reported from man. "Kalla" is a rebuke against seeking escape. "La wazar" means: no refuge. The exegetes explained it as a mountain. Mutarrif ibn al-Shikhkhir said: it was the refuge of the Arabs' flight in their lands, which is why it was used. The reality is that it is a refuge, whether a mountain, a fortress, a weapon, a man, or other than these. ("Ila rabbika yawma'idhin") means: to His judgment on that Day; you say, where is the escape? "Al-mustaqarr" means the state of settling, or the place of settling, of a garden or a fire, by His will, Exalted is He: He admits whom He wills to the Garden and admits whom He wills to the Fire.

﴿Bima qaddama wa-akhkhara﴾: Abdullah and Ibn Abbas said: by what he sent forward in his life and what he left behind of a sunnah that is practised after him. Ibn Abbas also said: by what he sent forward of sins and left behind of acts of obedience. Zayd ibn Aslam said: by what he sent forward of his wealth for himself, and what he left of it for the heir. Al-Nakha'i and Mujahid said: by the first of his deeds and the last of them. Al-Dahhak said: by what he sent forward of an obligation and left behind of an obligation. The apparent reading is to take it in its generality: He informs him of everything he sent forward and everything he left behind, both what the exegetes have mentioned and what they have not mentioned.

"Basirah": a predicate about man, meaning a witness. Qatadah said this, and the ha' is for emphasis. Al-Akhfash said: it is like your saying "fulan 'ibrah" and "hujjah" (so-and-so is a lesson and a proof). It was also said: it is feminine because he meant his limbs, meaning his limbs are a witness against himself. It was also said: "basirah" is a subject with an omitted noun, meaning "'ayn basirah" (a seeing eye), and "'ala nafsihi" is the predicate. The clause is in the place of the predicate about man, and the estimate is: a seeing eye. This is the view of al-Farra', who recited:

"As if upon the man of intellect there is a seeing eye, regarding his place, or a sight he is looking at."

"He is wary until he thinks all people, from fear, do not hide his secrets from them."

On this we prefer that "basirah" be the subject of the prepositional phrase, which is the predicate about man. Do you not see that it has been made the predicate about man by its position? On this view the ta' is the feminine marker. Ibn Abbas interpreted "al-basirah" as the limbs, or the guardian angels. The "ma'adhir" according to the majority means excuses, so the meaning is: even if he brings every excuse with which he defends himself, he is himself the witness against them and the clear proof against them. It was said that "ma'adhir" is the plural of "ma'dhirah." Al-Zamakhshari said: the analogical plural of "ma'dhirah" is "ma'adhir," so "ma'adhir" is not the plural of "ma'dhirah" but a collective noun for it, like "manakir" for "munkar." End of quote. This pattern is not among the patterns of collective nouns; it is among the patterns of broken plurals, like "madhakir" and "malamih," whose singulars are "lamhah" and "dhikr." No one has held that these two are collective nouns; rather it was said they are plurals of "lamhah" and "dhikr" by irregular formation, or they are plurals of a singular that was not spoken, namely "midhkar" and "malmahah." Al-Suddi and al-Dahhak said: "al-ma'adhir" means curtains, in the dialect of Yemen; its singular is "mi'dhar," which prevents seeing the one who is veiled, just as an excuse prevents the punishment for a sin. Al-Zajjaj also said this, meaning: even if he throws down veils intending to conceal his deed, his own self is a witness against him. They cited as evidence that "ma'adhir" means curtains the verse of the poet:

"But she grudged us a single hour at the abode, and she was hung above it with curtains."

It was said: "al-basirah" is the recording angels who write down whatever good or evil occurs, meaning: even if he conceals himself with coverings. If "ma'adhir" is taken from excuse, then the meaning of "wa-law alqa" is: he spoke his excuses and uttered them. It was said: even if he put forward his excuses and submitted. Al-Suddi said: even if he advanced a proof and an excuse. It was said: even if he shifted blame onto one another, as in His exalted saying: "Had you not been, we would have been believers" (Saba 31). "Al-'udhrah" and "al-'udhra" mean "al-ma'dhirah" (excuse). The poet said:

"Indeed, that is an excuse which, if it did not benefit..."

And he said concerning it: there is no excuse for one who denies.

Surah al-Qiyamah is Meccan and has forty verses.

In the name of Allah, the Most Gracious, the Most Merciful.

﴿I swear by the Day of Resurrection,﴾ ﴿and I swear by the self-reproaching soul.﴾ ﴿Does man think that We will not assemble his bones?﴾ ﴿Yes, We are able to put together even his fingertips.﴾ ﴿But man wants to continue in sin before him.﴾ ﴿He asks, "When is the Day of Resurrection?"﴾ ﴿So when the sight is dazzled,﴾ ﴿and the moon is eclipsed,﴾ ﴿and the sun and moon are joined together,﴾ ﴿on that day man will say, "Where is the escape?"﴾ ﴿No! There is no refuge.﴾ ﴿To your Lord, on that day, is the place of rest.﴾ ﴿On that day man will be informed of what he sent forward and what he left behind.﴾ ﴿Rather, man is a witness against himself,﴾ ﴿even if he presents his excuses.﴾ ﴿Do not move your tongue with it [the Qur'an] to hasten it.﴾ [al-Qiyamah: 16] ﴿Indeed, upon Us is its collection and its recitation.﴾ [al-Qiyamah: 17] ﴿So when We have recited it, follow its recitation.﴾ [al-Qiyamah: 18] ﴿Then upon Us is its explanation.﴾ [al-Qiyamah: 19] ﴿No! Rather, you love the hasty life [of this world].﴾ [al-Qiyamah: 20] ﴿And you neglect the Hereafter.﴾ [al-Qiyamah: 21] ﴿Faces on that day will be radiant,﴾ [al-Qiyamah: 22] ﴿looking toward their Lord.﴾ [al-Qiyamah: 23] ﴿And faces on that day will be frowning,﴾ [al-Qiyamah: 24] ﴿thinking that a calamity of the backbone is about to be inflicted upon them.﴾ [al-Qiyamah: 25] ﴿No! When [the soul] reaches the collarbones,﴾ [al-Qiyamah: 26] ﴿and it is said, "Who can cure him?"﴾ [al-Qiyamah: 27] ﴿and he thinks that it is the parting,﴾ [al-Qiyamah: 28] ﴿and the leg is entwined with the leg,﴾ [al-Qiyamah: 29] ﴿to your Lord on that day is the driving.﴾ [al-Qiyamah: 30] ﴿So he neither believed nor prayed,﴾ [al-Qiyamah: 31] ﴿but he denied and turned away.﴾ [al-Qiyamah: 32] ﴿Then he went to his family, swaggering.﴾ [al-Qiyamah: 33] ﴿Woe to you, and woe!﴾ [al-Qiyamah: 34] ﴿Again, woe to you, and woe!﴾ [al-Qiyamah: 35] ﴿Does man think that he will be left neglected?﴾ [al-Qiyamah: 36] ﴿Was he not a drop of semen emitted?﴾ [al-Qiyamah: 37] ﴿Then he became a clinging clot, and He created and proportioned [him],﴾ [al-Qiyamah: 38] ﴿and made of him two sexes, the male and the female.﴾ [al-Qiyamah: 39] ﴿Is not He able to give life to the dead?﴾ [al-Qiyamah: 40].

(Commentary) Bariqa, with a kasra on the ra', means he was frightened and bewildered. Its origin is from "bariqa al-rajul," when a man looked at lightning and his sight was dazzled. From this is the verse of Dhu al-Rummah:

"Even if Luqman the Wise were confronted, with Mayy unveiled before his eyes, he would nearly be dazzled."

Al-A'sha said:

"I used to see in the face of Mayya a glimpse, so I would be dazzled, fainting in my place."

Baraqa, with a fatha on the ra', means his sight was split; it comes from al-bariq (glitter), meaning his sight gleamed from the intensity of its staring. Al-wizr is what one takes refuge in, such as a fortress, a mountain, or other things. The poet said:

"By your life, there is no refuge for the youth from death, which overtakes him, and from old age."

Al-nadrah is blessing and the beauty and freshness of the complexion. The poet said:

"A grave that is never absent from my sight has come to me, and a blow of an axe over my head, a crushing one [fāqirah]."

That is: an effective one. Al-taraqi is the plural of taraqwah, which are the bones of the chest; each person has two taraqwahs, and it is the place of the death rattle. Duraid ibn al-Simmah said:

"How many a great matter have I defended on their behalf, when their souls had reached the collarbones."

Raqa yarqi, from al-ruqyah, is what is used to seek healing for the sick through words prepared for that purpose. Tamatta means he swaggered in his walk; its origin is from al-mata, which is the back, meaning he twisted his back in swaggering. It was also said: its origin is tamaṭṭaṭa, meaning he stretched in his walk and extended his shoulders; the ṭā' in it was changed to a weak letter (ḥarf ʿillah) out of dislike for the juxtaposition of similar letters, as they say tazannā from al-ẓann, whose origin is tazannana. Al-maṭīṭā is swaggering and the stretching of the hands while walking; al-maṭīṭ is the stagnant water at the bottom of a pool, because it stretches (yatamaṭṭaṭu) in it, meaning it extends. On this derivation, its origin is not from al-maṭṭ, because the two roots differ: the root of al-mata is (m-ṭ-w) and the root of tamaṭṭaṭa is (m-ṭ-ṭ). Sudan means neglected; it is said "ibil sudan," meaning camels left neglected, grazing wherever they wish without a herder. "Asdaytu al-shay'" means I neglected it, and "asdaytu hajati" means I wasted my need. The poet said:

"I swear by God with the utmost oath, that God has not created anything in vain [sudan]."

Abu Bakr ibn Duraid said in al-Maqsurah:

"I have not seen like the clouds, flocks of camels without markings, which you think are pastured while they are sudan (neglected)."

﴿I swear by the Day of Resurrection,﴾ ﴿and I swear by the self-reproaching soul.﴾ ﴿Does man think that We will not assemble his bones?﴾ ﴿Yes, We are able to put together even his fingertips.﴾ ﴿But man wants to continue in sin before him.﴾ ﴿He asks, "When is the Day of Resurrection?"﴾ ﴿So when the sight is dazzled,﴾ ﴿and the moon is eclipsed,﴾ ﴿and the sun and moon are joined together,﴾ ﴿on that day man will say, "Where is the escape?"﴾ ﴿No! There is no refuge.﴾ ﴿To your Lord, on that day, is the place of rest.﴾ ﴿On that day man will be informed of what he sent forward and what he left behind.﴾ ﴿Rather, man is a witness against himself,﴾ ﴿even if he presents his excuses.﴾ ﴿Do not move your tongue with it [the Qur'an] to hasten it.﴾ [al-Qiyamah: 16] ﴿Indeed, upon Us is its collection and its recitation.﴾ [al-Qiyamah: 17] ﴿So when We have recited it, follow its recitation.﴾ [al-Qiyamah: 18] ﴿Then upon Us is its explanation.﴾ [al-Qiyamah: 19] ﴿No! Rather, you love the hasty life [of this world].﴾ [al-Qiyamah: 20] ﴿And you neglect the Hereafter.﴾ [al-Qiyamah: 21] ﴿Faces on that day will be radiant,﴾ [al-Qiyamah: 22] ﴿looking toward their Lord.﴾ [al-Qiyamah: 23] ﴿And faces on that day will be frowning,﴾ [al-Qiyamah: 24] ﴿thinking that a calamity of the backbone is about to be inflicted upon them.﴾ [al-Qiyamah: 25] ﴿No! When [the soul] reaches the collarbones,﴾ [al-Qiyamah: 26] ﴿and it is said, "Who can cure him?"﴾ [al-Qiyamah: 27] ﴿and he thinks that it is the parting,﴾ [al-Qiyamah: 28] ﴿and the leg is entwined with the leg,﴾ [al-Qiyamah: 29] ﴿to your Lord on that day is the driving.﴾ [al-Qiyamah: 30] ﴿So he neither believed nor prayed,﴾ [al-Qiyamah: 31] ﴿but he denied and turned away.﴾ [al-Qiyamah: 32] ﴿Then he went to his family, swaggering.﴾ [al-Qiyamah: 33] ﴿Woe to you, and woe!﴾ [al-Qiyamah: 34] ﴿Again, woe to you, and woe!﴾ [al-Qiyamah: 35] ﴿Does man think that he will be left neglected?﴾ [al-Qiyamah: 36] ﴿Was he not a drop of semen emitted?﴾ [al-Qiyamah: 37] ﴿Then he became a clinging clot, and He created and proportioned [him],﴾ [al-Qiyamah: 38] ﴿and made of him two sexes, the male and the female.﴾ [al-Qiyamah: 39] ﴿Is not He able to give life to the dead?﴾ [al-Qiyamah: 40].

This surah is Meccan, and its connection to what precedes it is that at the end of the previous surah He says: ﴿No! Rather, they do not fear the Hereafter.﴾ [al-Muddaththir: 53] ﴿No! Indeed, it is a reminder.﴾ [al-Muddaththir: 54] It contains much about the conditions of the Resurrection, so here He mentions the Day of Resurrection and some of its conditions. The discussion of ﴿I do not swear﴾ has already been covered, as well as the disagreement over "lā" and the disagreement over its readings at the end of al-Waqi'ah. God swore by the Day of Resurrection because of its greatness and terror. As for ﴿lā uqsimu﴾, it has been said that "lā" is negative: He denies that He swears by the self-reproaching soul, and swears by the Day of Resurrection; al-Hasan stated this. The majority hold that God swore by both things.

As for al-lawwāmah, al-Hasan said it is the one that blames its owner for abandoning obedience and similar matters; in this sense it is praiseworthy, and that is why God swore by it. Something similar is reported from Ibn 'Abbas and Mujahid: it blames for what has passed and regrets evil, asking why it did it, and regrets good, asking why it did not increase it. It was also said that it is the God-fearing soul that blames souls on the Day of Resurrection for their shortcomings in piety. Ibn 'Abbas and Qatadah said it is the wicked, disquieted soul that blames its owner for what he missed of the worldly striving and its goods; in this sense it is blameworthy, and it is fitting that the oath by it be negated. Al-nafs al-lawwamah is a generic noun with this attribute. It was also said that it is a specific soul, namely the soul of Adam, peace be upon him, which never ceased to blame him for his action that caused his expulsion from the Garden. Ibn 'Atiyyah said: every soul that is intermediate, neither at peace nor commanding evil, is lawwamah in both directions: at times it blames for abandoning obedience, and at times it blames for missing what it desires. When it becomes at peace, it becomes pure and clear. End of quote.

The connection between the two oaths lies in the states of the soul, its happiness and its wretchedness, and the manifestation of that on the Day of Resurrection. The answer to the oath is omitted, and what indicates it is the Day of Resurrection, which is sworn by, and what follows it in His words: ﴿Does man think﴾, and its estimated meaning is: "You will surely be resurrected."

Al-Zamakhshari said: If you say, God's words ﴿But no, by your Lord, they do not believe﴾ [al-Nisa': 65], and the verses you recited, the sworn matter in them is negated, and he had recited the words of Imru' al-Qays:

"No, by your father, daughter of al-'Amiri, the people do not claim that I flee."

And the words of Ghuwayyah ibn Sulma:

"Umamah called out, to burden me, so let me not care."

He said: Why did you not claim that the "lā" used for the oath was added as a preface to negation after it and as its emphasis, and estimate the omitted sworn matter here as negative, like your saying: ﴿I do not swear by the Day of Resurrection﴾, you will not be left neglected? I said: If they had restricted the matter to negation without affirmation, this statement would have had some basis, but He did not swear. Do you not see how He linked ﴿I do not swear by this city﴾ [al-Balad: 1] with His words ﴿Certainly We created man in hardship﴾ [al-Balad: 4]? And similarly ﴿So I do not swear by the positions of the stars﴾ [al-Waqi'ah: 75] ﴿Indeed, it is a noble Qur'an﴾ [al-Waqi'ah: 77]? Then al-Zamakhshari said: The answer to the oath is what His words ﴿Does man think that We will not assemble his bones﴾ indicate, and it is: "you will surely be resurrected." End of quote. This is also the estimate of al-Nahhas. The view of one who said the answer to the oath is ﴿Does man think﴾, and what is reported from al-Hasan that the answer is ﴿Yes, We are able﴾, and what was said that "lā" in both oaths is for negating them, meaning "I do not swear about anything," and that the estimate is "I ask you: does man think?", are sayings not fit to be adopted; rather they are discarded and paper should not be blackened with them. Had they not been recorded in books, I would not have pointed them out.

Al-insan here means the disbelieving denier of the Resurrection. It is reported that 'Adi ibn Rabi'ah said to the Messenger of God ﷺ: "O Muhammad, tell me about the Day of Resurrection: when will its matter be?" The Messenger of God ﷺ informed him, and he said: "Had I witnessed that day, I would not (p-385) have believed you or believed in it, or [do you claim] that God will gather these bones after their decay?" Then it was revealed. It was also said that it was revealed concerning Abu Jahl, who used to say: "Does Muhammad claim that God will gather these bones after their decay and dispersal, and restore them as a new creation?"

The majority read ﴿najma'a﴾ with "n" and ﴿'izāmahu﴾ in the accusative. Qatadah read it with "t", in the passive voice, and ﴿'izāmuhu﴾ in the nominative; the meaning is: after their dispersal, their mixing with the dust, and the winds scattering them to the far ends of the earth.

His words ﴿Does man think﴾ are an interrogative of affirmation and reproach, in which he denies God's power to restore what is non-existent. ﴿Balā﴾ is the answer to the interrogative that extends to the negation, meaning: "Yes, We will gather them." He mentioned the bones, although the meaning is the restoration of the person and the gathering of his scattered parts, because the bones are the mold of creation.

The majority read ﴿qādirīn﴾ with the accusative as a state (ḥāl) of the pronoun in the implied verb, which is "yajma'uhā" (He gathers them). Ibn Abi 'Abla and Ibn al-Sumayqa read ﴿qādirūn﴾, meaning "We are able."

﴿To put together his fingertips﴾: these are the fingers, the bones most scattered and most finely divided, the bones in the fingertips and their joints; this is at the resurrection. Ibn 'Abbas and the majority said the meaning is: We will make them in his present life a single piece, or a single bone like a camel's sole, with no separations in it, meaning in this world, so that his benefit from them becomes small. This view contains a threat. The first meaning is the apparent one and the intended purpose of the arrangement of the speech. Al-Zamakhshari mentioned these two views with polished wording, in keeping with his habit of relating the views of earlier scholars. It was also said: ﴿qādirīn﴾ is accusative as the predicate of "kāna," meaning: "Yes, we were able at the beginning."

Nay, but man desires to continue in sin (lit. "Nay, but man wishes"): "Bal" (nay, but) is a particle of disengagement (idrab), which is a transition from one statement to another without negating the first. The apparent sense is that "yurid" (desires) is a report about what man desires. Al-Zamakhshari said: "Bal yurid" is coordinated with "ayahsabu" (does man think...), so it may be preceded by an interrogative and may be affirmative, turning away from one questioned matter to another, or turning away from a questioned matter to an affirmative one. End of quote. These three estimations do not appear clearly; they are forced. Rather, the meaning is a report about man without negating the content of the preceding sentence, which is "We are able to gather his bones" (cf. verse 4), in order to show what man is like: his lack of thought about the Hereafter and that he is preoccupied with his desires. The object of "yurid" is omitted, indicated by the causal clause in "liyafjura" (so that he may commit wickedness). Mujahid, al-Hasan, Ikrimah, Ibn Jubayr, al-Dahhak and al-Suddi said: the meaning of the verse is that man only desires his lusts and his sins, so that he may continue in them forever, heedlessly driving forward, obeying his hopes and postponing repentance. Al-Suddi also said: so that he may do wrong to the extent of his capacity. On this view the pronoun in "amamahu" (before him) refers to man, which is the apparent reading. Ibn Abbas said something implying that the pronoun refers to the Day of Resurrection: that man, during his lifetime, is "amam" (in front of) the Day of Resurrection, and "bayna yadayhi" (before him) is the Day of Resurrection, behind him. So he desires his lusts, so that he may commit wickedness by denying the resurrection and other matters before the Day of Resurrection, and he does not know the state he is in. "Al-amam" (in front) is a noun of place, here used metaphorically for time, meaning: so that he may commit wickedness in what lies before him and awaits him of the time of his life.

﴿Yas'alu ayyana yawmu al-qiyamah﴾ means: when is the Day of Resurrection? It is a question of mockery, denial and obstinacy. The majority read "baraqa" with a kasra on the ra'. Zayd ibn Thabit, Nasr ibn Asim, Abdullah ibn Abi Ishaq, Abu Haywah, Ibn Abi Ablah, al-Za'farani, Ibn Miqsam, Nafi', Zayd ibn Ali, Aban on the authority of Asim, Harun and Mahbub (both on the authority of Abu Amr), al-Hasan and al-Jahdari read it with a fatha, in differing reports from them. Abu Ubaydah said: "baraqa" with a fatha means "shaqqa" (split). Ibn Ishaq said: it means "khafata" (was dazzled) at death. Mujahid said: this is at death. Al-Hasan said: it is the Day of Resurrection. Abu al-Sammal read "balaqa" with a lam in place of the ra', meaning "infataha" (opened) and "infaraja" (parted). It is said: "balaqa al-bab" and "ablaqtuhu" and "ballaqtuhu," meaning I opened it. This is the view of the lexicographers, except al-Farra', who says "balaqahu" and "ablaqahu" mean he closed it. Tha'lab said: al-Farra' erred in this; it is only "balaqa al-bab" and "ablaqahu" when he opened it. End of quote. It is possible that the lam is a substitute for the ra', as they interchange in some speech, as in their saying "nathara" and "nathala," and "wajara" and "wajila."

﴿Wa-khasafa al-qamar﴾: the majority read it in the active voice. Abu Haywah, Ibn Abi Ablah, Yazid ibn Qutayb and Zayd ibn Ali read it in the passive voice. It is said: "khasafa al-qamar" and "khasafahu Allah," and likewise for the sun. Abu Ubaydah and a group of lexicographers said: "khusuf" and "kusuf" have the same meaning. Ibn Abi Uways said: "kusuf" is the going of part of the light, and "khusuf" is all of it.

﴿Wa-jumi'a al-shamsu wal-qamar﴾: the feminine marker was not attached, because the feminine of the sun is metaphorical, or because of giving precedence to the masculine over the feminine. Al-Kisa'i said: it was construed according to meaning, the estimate being: the two lights or the two radiances were gathered. As for the meaning of their being gathered together, Ata' ibn Yasar said: they will be gathered and cast into the Fire. And on his authority: they will be gathered on the Day of Resurrection and then thrown into the sea, and they will become the great Fire of God. It was said: they will be gathered together in rising from the west, rising black and folded up. Ali and Ibn Abbas said: they will be placed in the light of the veils. It was said: they will come together and not separate, and they will draw near to people so that sweat will overtake them because of the intensity of the heat; the meaning is that their heat is gathered. It was also said: they will be gathered together in the loss of light, so there will be no alternation of night and day.

The majority read "al-mafarr" with a fatha on the mim and the fa': where is the escape? Al-Hasan ibn Ali ibn Abi Talib, al-Hasan ibn Zayd, Ibn Abbas, al-Hasan, Ikrimah, Ayyub al-Sakhtiyani, Kulthum ibn Iyad, Mujahid, Ibn Ya'mur, Hammad ibn Salamah, Abu Raja', Isa, Ibn Abi Ishaq, Abu Haywah, Ibn Abi Ablah and al-Zuhri read it with a kasra on the fa', which denotes the place of escape. Al-Hasan read it with a kasra on the mim and a fatha on the fa'; Ibn Atiyah attributed this to al-Zuhri, meaning one who escapes well. This pattern is most often used for instruments and for descriptions of horses, as in the saying of the poet:

"Charging, fleeing, advancing, retreating, all together."

The apparent reading is that His saying "Kalla la wazar" (Nay! There is no refuge) and "Ila rabbika yawma'idhin al-mustaqarr" (To your Lord on that Day is the place of rest) are part of the speech of man. It was also said that they are part of the speech of God, not reported from man. "Kalla" is a rebuke against seeking escape. "La wazar" means: no refuge. The exegetes explained it as a mountain. Mutarrif ibn al-Shikhkhir said: it was the refuge of the Arabs' flight in their lands, which is why it was used. The reality is that it is a refuge, whether a mountain, a fortress, a weapon, a man, or other than these. ("Ila rabbika yawma'idhin") means: to His judgment on that Day; you say, where is the escape? "Al-mustaqarr" means the state of settling, or the place of settling, of a garden or a fire, by His will, Exalted is He: He admits whom He wills to the Garden and admits whom He wills to the Fire.

﴿Bima qaddama wa-akhkhara﴾: Abdullah and Ibn Abbas said: by what he sent forward in his life and what he left behind of a sunnah that is practised after him. Ibn Abbas also said: by what he sent forward of sins and left behind of acts of obedience. Zayd ibn Aslam said: by what he sent forward of his wealth for himself, and what he left of it for the heir. Al-Nakha'i and Mujahid said: by the first of his deeds and the last of them. Al-Dahhak said: by what he sent forward of an obligation and left behind of an obligation. The apparent reading is to take it in its generality: He informs him of everything he sent forward and everything he left behind, both what the exegetes have mentioned and what they have not mentioned.

"Basirah": a predicate about man, meaning a witness. Qatadah said this, and the ha' is for emphasis. Al-Akhfash said: it is like your saying "fulan 'ibrah" and "hujjah" (so-and-so is a lesson and a proof). It was also said: it is feminine because he meant his limbs, meaning his limbs are a witness against himself. It was also said: "basirah" is a subject with an omitted noun, meaning "'ayn basirah" (a seeing eye), and "'ala nafsihi" is the predicate. The clause is in the place of the predicate about man, and the estimate is: a seeing eye. This is the view of al-Farra', who recited:

"As if upon the man of intellect there is a seeing eye, regarding his place, or a sight he is looking at."

"He is wary until he thinks all people, from fear, do not hide his secrets from them."

On this we prefer that "basirah" be the subject of the prepositional phrase, which is the predicate about man. Do you not see that it has been made the predicate about man by its position? On this view the ta' is the feminine marker. Ibn Abbas interpreted "al-basirah" as the limbs, or the guardian angels. The "ma'adhir" according to the majority means excuses, so the meaning is: even if he brings every excuse with which he defends himself, he is himself the witness against them and the clear proof against them. It was said that "ma'adhir" is the plural of "ma'dhirah." Al-Zamakhshari said: the analogical plural of "ma'dhirah" is "ma'adhir," so "ma'adhir" is not the plural of "ma'dhirah" but a collective noun for it, like "manakir" for "munkar." End of quote. This pattern is not among the patterns of collective nouns; it is among the patterns of broken plurals, like "madhakir" and "malamih," whose singulars are "lamhah" and "dhikr." No one has held that these two are collective nouns; rather it was said they are plurals of "lamhah" and "dhikr" by irregular formation, or they are plurals of a singular that was not spoken, namely "midhkar" and "malmahah." Al-Suddi and al-Dahhak said: "al-ma'adhir" means curtains, in the dialect of Yemen; its singular is "mi'dhar," which prevents seeing the one who is veiled, just as an excuse prevents the punishment for a sin. Al-Zajjaj also said this, meaning: even if he throws down veils intending to conceal his deed, his own self is a witness against him. They cited as evidence that "ma'adhir" means curtains the verse of the poet:

"But she grudged us a single hour at the abode, and she was hung above it with curtains."

It was said: "al-basirah" is the recording angels who write down whatever good or evil occurs, meaning: even if he conceals himself with coverings. If "ma'adhir" is taken from excuse, then the meaning of "wa-law alqa" is: he spoke his excuses and uttered them. It was said: even if he put forward his excuses and submitted.
